fixes.explanation: A donkey it is, friend. Jesus says they'll find one tied there, with her colt beside her (Matthew 21:2). He tells them to untie both and bring them to Him. Two animals, one errand, and the disciples get the whole plan before they even leave.

A governor sounds official, friend, but the prophet uses a bigger word. He says, “See, your King comes to you…” (Matthew 21:5) The one coming to the Daughter of Zion is her King. Not a governor, not an army, a King.

Gentle, friend! The prophet says the King comes “…gentle and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey.” (Matthew 21:5) Kings usually show up with a big loud entrance, so I think a gentle King on a donkey is a surprise. That's the word the text picks for Him.

Not quite, friend. It's False. The text says they “…laid their cloaks on them, and Jesus sat on them.” (Matthew 21:7) The cloaks go on the animals, and Jesus is sitting on them. That matches what the prophet said, a King riding on a donkey (Matthew 21:5).

Cloaks AND branches, friend! “A massive crowd spread their cloaks on the road, while others cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road.” (Matthew 21:8) Some spread cloaks, and others cut branches from the trees. Both of them end up on the road for Jesus.

That sounds fancy, friend, but it's not in the text. “A massive crowd spread their cloaks on the road, while others cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road.” (Matthew 21:8) Cloaks and cut branches, that's what covers the road. Flowers and fine linen don't get a mention.

Golden coins on the road, friend? That would stop traffic! But the text says, “A massive crowd spread their cloaks on the road, while others cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road.” (Matthew 21:8) Cloaks and branches, nothing shiny.
The Son of David, friend! The crowds shout, “Hosanna to the Son of David!” (Matthew 21:9) Those in front of Him and those behind Him are shouting. That's the first line the text gives.
It's False, friend. The whole city is stirred, and they ask, “Who is this?” (Matthew 21:10) That's a question about who He is. The crowds give the answer in the next verse (Matthew 21:11).
False is right, friend! When Jesus enters, the whole city is stirred and asks, “Who is this?” (Matthew 21:10) That's a city asking about Him. The crowds reply in the next verse (Matthew 21:11).

Close on the shape, friend, but the details are off. The crowds reply, “This is Jesus, the prophet from Nazareth in Galilee.” (Matthew 21:11) They say prophet, and they say Nazareth. Bethany and Judea aren't in their answer.
